```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(bayesDP)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%", fig.align = "center", dpi = 150)
```

# Purpose and current limitations

`bdpsurvival()` uses piecewise constant hazards for right-censored outcomes. In one arm, the estimand is survival probability at a specified time. With two arms, the reported effect is an approximate common log hazard ratio, treatment relative to control.

The baseline-prior contribution during historical augmentation remains under investigation ([issue 17](https://github.com/graemeleehickey/bayesDP/issues/17)). The implemented update is described below. These examples illustrate the calculations and their sensitivity to the borrowing method; they do not establish operating characteristics for a trial design.

See the [borrowing overview](borrowing.html) for weighting choices and interpretation. The main examples use `method = "fixed"` for exposition and then compare it with the default `method = "mc"`.

# Data and follow-up

Supply current and historical data frames with compatible columns. Use `Surv(time, status) ~ 1` for a one-arm analysis, or `Surv(time, status) ~ treatment` for two arms. Code `status = 1` for an event and `status = 0` for right censoring; `time` is the observed event or censoring time. For two arms, code `treatment = 1` and control as 0, and provide both arms in both studies for the examples below. Additional covariate adjustment is not implemented.

Choose a time unit, clinically relevant survival horizon, and interval boundaries. `breaks` contains positive internal cutpoints, without zero or infinity. The final interval extends beyond the last cutpoint; `breaks = numeric(0)` specifies one constant hazard. Cutpoints are sorted and duplicates removed.

By default the cutpoints are the pooled observed-time 20th, 40th, 60th, and 80th percentiles; these are quantiles of event-or-censoring times, not estimated survival quantiles. The examples prespecify cutpoints and the horizon.

# One-arm example with censoring

We simulate event times with mean 10 months for 60 current participants and mean 11 months for 100 historical participants. Independent censoring times have mean 18 months, with additional administrative censoring at 18 months. The observed time is the minimum of event and censoring times.

```{r censored-data}
simulate_followup <- function(n, mean_event, mean_censor, horizon) {
  event_time <- rexp(n, rate = 1 / mean_event)
  censor_time <- pmin(rexp(n, rate = 1 / mean_censor), horizon)
  data.frame(time = pmin(event_time, censor_time),
    status = as.integer(event_time <= censor_time))
}
set.seed(42)
current <- simulate_followup(60, mean_event = 10, mean_censor = 18, horizon = 18)
historical <- simulate_followup(100, mean_event = 11, mean_censor = 18, horizon = 18)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  source = c("Current", "Historical"),
  participants = c(nrow(current), nrow(historical)),
  events = c(sum(current$status), sum(historical$status)),
  censored = c(sum(current$status == 0), sum(historical$status == 0))
))
```

```{r survival-fits}
set.seed(42)
current_only <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = current, data0 = historical, breaks = c(3, 6, 12), surv_time = 6,
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "fixed", fix_alpha = TRUE, alpha_max = 0)
set.seed(42)
discounted <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = current, data0 = historical, breaks = c(3, 6, 12), surv_time = 6,
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "fixed", fix_alpha = FALSE, alpha_max = 1)
set.seed(42)
full_borrowing <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = current, data0 = historical, breaks = c(3, 6, 12), surv_time = 6,
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "fixed", fix_alpha = TRUE, alpha_max = 1)
fits <- list("Current only" = current_only, "Discounted" = discounted,
  "Full borrowing" = full_borrowing)
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, function(fit) {
  arm <- fit$posterior_treatment
  c(alpha = arm$alpha_discount, median = median(arm$posterior_survival),
    lower = unname(quantile(arm$posterior_survival, 0.025)),
    upper = unname(quantile(arm$posterior_survival, 0.975)))
}))
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4,
  col.names = c("Historical weight", "Median S(6)", "Lower 95% CrI", "Upper 95% CrI"))
```

The estimated historical weight is `r round(discounted$posterior_treatment$alpha_discount, 4)`. The augmented posterior median six-month survival is `r round(median(discounted$posterior_treatment$posterior_survival), 4)`. These summarize survival probability at six months, not median survival time. The full-borrowing result includes the extra baseline-prior contribution described below and should not be called an ordinary pooled analysis.

`print()` gives a compact summary at the requested horizon. Its sample size and event count refer to current participants. The longer `summary()` table reports risk sets immediately before each observed event or censoring time, alongside posterior median survival, posterior SDs, and 95% equal-tailed credible intervals. Splitting follow-up into hazard intervals does not create additional participants or observation times. These risk sets describe the observed current cohort; historical borrowing changes the survival estimates, not the numbers at risk.

```{r one-arm-summary}
print(discounted)
```

```{r survival-curves, fig.cap="Posterior median survival curves for the estimated-borrowing fit. These are model-based curves, not Kaplan–Meier estimates; uncertainty is summarized in the six-month table.", fig.alt="Posterior median survival curves for the estimated-borrowing fit. These are model-based curves, not Kaplan–Meier estimates; uncertainty is summarized in the six-month table."}
plot(discounted, type = "survival", print = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Follow-up (months)")
```

## Sensitivity to the borrowing method

Keep the data, priors, intervals, horizon, discount function, and maximum weight the same, and change the borrowing procedure. For the draw-specific method, summarize the distribution of weights as well as the survival estimate. The weight percentiles describe variation introduced by this procedure; they are not a credible interval from a separate posterior model for the weight.

```{r survival-method-comparison}
set.seed(42)
discounted_mc <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = current, data0 = historical, breaks = c(3, 6, 12), surv_time = 6,
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "mc", fix_alpha = FALSE,
  discount_function = "identity", alpha_max = 1)
format_interval <- function(x) paste(sprintf("%.3f", quantile(x, c(.025, .975))), collapse = " to ")
methods_one <- list("Fixed" = discounted, "Draw-specific" = discounted_mc)
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(methods_one), function(method) {
  arm <- methods_one[[method]]$posterior_treatment
  data.frame(Method = method, `Median weight` = median(arm$alpha_discount),
    `Weight 2.5–97.5%` = format_interval(arm$alpha_discount),
    `Median S(6)` = median(arm$posterior_survival),
    `95% CrI for S(6)` = format_interval(arm$posterior_survival), check.names = FALSE)
})), digits = 3)
```

The two procedures need not give the same mean or median weight, even with many simulation draws. Their definitions differ: one transforms an estimated directional probability, whereas the other transforms each standardized difference. Neither weight is the posterior probability of equivalence between studies.

# Two-arm example

Add independent current and historical controls with mean event time 12 months, using the same censoring mechanism. All four sources are present.

```{r two-arm-survival}
set.seed(101)
control <- simulate_followup(60, mean_event = 12, mean_censor = 18, horizon = 18)
control0 <- simulate_followup(100, mean_event = 12, mean_censor = 18, horizon = 18)
current_two <- rbind(transform(current, treatment = 1), transform(control, treatment = 0))
historical_two <- rbind(transform(historical, treatment = 1), transform(control0, treatment = 0))
set.seed(42)
fit_two <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ treatment,
  data = current_two, data0 = historical_two, breaks = c(3, 6, 12),
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "fixed", fix_alpha = FALSE, alpha_max = 1)
summary(fit_two)
log_hr <- as.numeric(fit_two$final$posterior_loghazard)
knitr::kable(rbind(
  "Log hazard ratio" = quantile(log_hr, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),
  "Hazard ratio" = quantile(exp(log_hr), c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
), digits = 4)
```

The summary counts `r nrow(current)` current treatment participants and `r nrow(control)` current control participants, regardless of how many intervals their follow-up spans. The treatment and control historical weights are `r round(fit_two$posterior_treatment$alpha_discount, 4)` and `r round(fit_two$posterior_control$alpha_discount, 4)`, respectively. The median hazard ratio is `r round(median(exp(log_hr)), 4)`. For an adverse event, a hazard ratio below 1 favours treatment; the corresponding no-effect value on the log scale is zero. The two rows transform both the estimates and credible limits consistently.

```{r hazard-ratio, fig.cap="Posterior hazard ratio from the approximate common-effect calculation. The dashed line marks a hazard ratio of 1.", fig.alt="Posterior hazard ratio from the approximate common-effect calculation. The dashed line marks a hazard ratio of 1."}
ggplot(data.frame(hazard_ratio = exp(log_hr)), aes(hazard_ratio)) +
  geom_density(colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "#666666") +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = "Hazard ratio (treatment / control)", y = "Density")
```

Repeat the two-arm analysis using draw-specific borrowing, retaining the same settings. Treatment and control have separate weight distributions.

```{r two-arm-method-comparison}
set.seed(42)
fit_two_mc <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ treatment,
  data = current_two, data0 = historical_two, breaks = c(3, 6, 12),
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "mc", fix_alpha = FALSE,
  discount_function = "identity", alpha_max = 1)
methods_two <- list("Fixed" = fit_two, "Draw-specific" = fit_two_mc)
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(methods_two), function(method) {
  fit <- methods_two[[method]]
  hr <- exp(fit$final$posterior_loghazard)
  data.frame(Method = method,
    `Median treatment weight` = median(fit$posterior_treatment$alpha_discount),
    `Median control weight` = median(fit$posterior_control$alpha_discount),
    `Median HR` = median(hr), `95% CrI for HR` = format_interval(hr), check.names = FALSE)
})), digits = 3)
```

# Piecewise exponential model

Partition follow-up at $0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_J=\infty$. For the event-counting convention used when splitting records, interval $j$ is $(\tau_{j-1},\tau_j]$. Let $d_{ij}$ indicate an event in that interval and $t_{ij}$ be exposure *within* the interval, not total follow-up. Define $D_j=\sum_i d_{ij}$ and $T_j=\sum_i t_{ij}$.

The hazard is constant at $\lambda_j$ in interval $j$. Independent Gamma priors with shape $a_0$ and rate $b_0$ give

$$
\lambda_j\mid D_j,T_j\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_0+D_j,b_0+T_j).
$$

The defaults are $a_0=b_0=0.1$. This prior is not flat. The rate parameter has exposure-time units, so a change from months to days requires a corresponding change in $b_0$ to preserve the same prior information.

Let $\ell_j(t)=\max\{0,\min(t,\tau_j)-\tau_{j-1}\}$ be the length of interval $j$ before $t$. Then

$$
S(t)=\exp\left\{-\sum_j\lambda_j\ell_j(t)\right\}.
$$

The exported helper `ppexp(t, hazards, cuts = c(0, breaks))` returns $1-S(t)$ for each row of hazard draws. The fitting function calculates survival directly from cumulative hazards. Borrowing comparisons use retained log hazards, so they can distinguish draws even when the corresponding survival probabilities round to zero or one.

## Comparing current and historical data

Comparisons use independent draws from the separate current and historical posteriors within an arm. Write $A_j=a_0+D_j$ and $B_j=b_0+T_j$, with $A_{0j},B_{0j}$ defined analogously for historical data. Gamma shape-rate moments give $\operatorname{Var}(\lambda_j)=A_j/B_j^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\log\lambda_j)=\psi_1(A_j)$, where $\psi_1$ is the trigamma function [@wellner2008]. The latter is exact; replacing it by $1/A_j$ is unsuitable for small shapes.

### One arm: survival at the chosen horizon

At horizon $t^*$, the log survival difference and its posterior variance are

$$
\Delta^{(s)}=\log S^{(s)}(t^*)-\log S_0^{(s)}(t^*)
=\sum_j\ell_j(t^*)\{\lambda_{0j}^{(s)}-\lambda_j^{(s)}\},
$$

$$
V=\sum_j\ell_j(t^*)^2\left(\frac{A_j}{B_j^2}+\frac{A_{0j}}{B_{0j}^2}\right),
\qquad Z^{(s)}=\frac{\Delta^{(s)}}{\sqrt{V}}.
$$

Only intervals before the horizon contribute. For example, a horizon at a cutpoint excludes the subsequent interval. Changing the horizon can change the comparison, although the resulting historical weight is applied to all intervals.

### Two arms: compare studies separately within each arm

Within treatment, and separately within control, define the interval log hazard differences and variances

$$
C_j^{(s)}=\log\lambda_{0j}^{(s)}-\log\lambda_j^{(s)},
\qquad v_j=\psi_1(A_{0j})+\psi_1(A_j).
$$

Combine intervals using inverse-variance weights:

$$
C^{(s)}=\frac{\sum_j C_j^{(s)}/v_j}{\sum_j1/v_j},
\qquad V=\frac{1}{\sum_j1/v_j},
\qquad Z^{(s)}=\frac{C^{(s)}}{\sqrt{V}}.
$$

Both borrowing methods use these analytic interval weights. Opposing current–historical differences across intervals can cancel in the combined comparison; inspect interval-specific hazards rather than treating a high weight as evidence of agreement throughout follow-up.

### Transforming the comparison into a weight

For `method = "fixed"`, estimate the directional probability $q=\Pr\{\Delta>0\mid\text{data}\}$ for one arm, or $q=\Pr\{C>0\mid\text{data}\}$ within each arm of a two-arm analysis. Then use

$$
p=2\min(q,1-q),\qquad \alpha=\alpha_{\max}W(p).
$$

For `method = "mc"`, use each standardized draw directly:

$$
p^{(s)}=2\{1-\Phi(|Z^{(s)}|)\},
\qquad \alpha^{(s)}=\alpha_{\max}W(p^{(s)}).
$$

The normal-tail transformation is applied once: $Z^{(s)}=0$ gives $p^{(s)}=1$, and larger absolute differences give smaller values. It remains an approximate comparison score, particularly with sparse, skewed Gamma posteriors; exact variance standardization does not make those distributions normal. Identical current and historical data produce independent posterior draws, so their draw-specific weights need not all equal one.

Neither transformation is a posterior probability of equality or equivalence. `p_hat` contains the selected method's transformed comparison, including when `fix_alpha = TRUE`. In that case, the weight is prescribed as `alpha_max` and does not depend on `p_hat`.

Log-Gamma sampling avoids an artificial positive hazard offset. Very small hazards may still round to zero in the returned ordinary-scale matrices, while their retained log values remain available for the comparisons and treatment effect. More simulation draws reduce Monte Carlo error; they do not remove the spread of draw-specific weights or resolve the normal approximation's limitations.

## Implemented historical augmentation

For each weight, the current implementation generates augmented hazards as

$$
\lambda_j\mid\text{data},\alpha\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\left(
(1+\alpha)a_0+D_j+\alpha D_{0j},
(1+\alpha)b_0+T_j+\alpha T_{0j}\right).
$$

It discounts the historical posterior parameters, including their baseline-prior terms. A historical-likelihood power update would instead include $a_0,b_0$ only once [@haddad2017]. The intended construction is under review in issue 17. This distinction matters most when event counts or exposure are small, or the prior is influential. In two arms, the implementation uses separate treatment and control weights in this same update.

With `method = "mc"`, substitute $\alpha^{(s)}$ for each draw. The resulting marginal distribution mixes over the generated weights and is generally not one Gamma distribution.

## Approximate two-arm effect

From the augmented arm hazards, calculate for each draw

$$
R_j^{(s)}=\log\lambda_{jT}^{(s)}-\log\lambda_{jC}^{(s)},
\qquad V_j=\operatorname{Var}_s(R_j^{(s)}),
$$

and combine intervals as

$$
\beta^{(s)}=\frac{\sum_j R_j^{(s)}/V_j}{\sum_j1/V_j}.
$$

These empirical variances summarize the *augmented* draws, including variation from draw-specific weights. They serve a different purpose from the analytic source-posterior variances used to choose borrowing weights above.

This is the implemented inverse-variance approximation to a common log hazard ratio. It is not an exact joint posterior fit of a proportional-hazards Poisson regression. A common treatment effect across intervals is needed for a common-hazard-ratio interpretation; with time-varying effects it is a precision-weighted summary. Large-event approximations such as $1/D_{jT}+1/D_{jC}$ do not describe the implemented empirical variances exactly and are unsuitable when an interval has no events.

# Assumptions and sensitivity

Assume independent participants and censoring independent of the event process within each modeled group. Use the same event definition, time origin, and time units across studies. Inspect follow-up support at the chosen horizon; extrapolation beyond observed follow-up depends on the piecewise hazard assumptions.

Check sensitivity to interval boundaries, survival horizon, Gamma priors, borrowing method, discount function, and maximum weight. Sparse or zero-event intervals can be strongly prior-dependent. Compare interval-specific effects before interpreting a common hazard ratio, and check numerical precision with more draws and independent seeds.

Trial-design use requires evaluation of the complete procedure, including its operating characteristics under agreement and conflict between studies. The baseline-prior augmentation question in issue 17 remains unresolved; these worked examples do not provide that validation.
